description: Phase 6aj gate — column alias (AS name) visible in GROUP BY / ORDER BY / HAVING. Matches SQLite's alias-resolution semantics.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (3, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3);
SELECT a AS x FROM t ORDER BY x;
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 10), (1, 20), (2, 30);
SELECT a AS grp, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY grp ORDER BY grp;
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 10), (1, 20), (2, 30);
SELECT a AS grp, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM t GROUP BY a HAVING cnt > 1 ORDER BY grp;

cases.name: alias-in-order-by-expr
cases.description: Alias of an expression (not just column ref) works in ORDER BY.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (3), (1), (2);
SELECT a * 10 AS scaled FROM t ORDER BY scaled;

cases.name: alias-shadows-column-in-order-by
cases.description: When an alias has the same name as a real column, ORDER BY resolves to the alias (projection-level scope wins).

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 30), (2, 20), (3, 10);
SELECT b AS a FROM t ORDER BY a;

cases.name: alias-not-in-where
cases.description: WHERE is evaluated before projection; aliases are NOT visible there.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3);
SELECT a AS x FROM t WHERE x > 1;

cases.name: alias-ambiguous-if-duplicate
cases.description: Two projections with the same alias cannot be referenced from ORDER BY — ambiguous.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 10);
SELECT a AS x, b AS x FROM t ORDER BY x;

cases.name: distinct-having-alias-shadows-column
cases.description: Task #92 regression — SELECT DISTINCT ... AS col_name ... HAVING col_name ... where the alias shadows a real column. Under DISTINCT, HAVING must resolve the shadowed name to the base-table column, not the aliased expression. Before the fix, leap-rust rewrote `+col1` to `+(-col1)` = -81 and kept the (24,81) group; leap-c correctly resolved `+col1` to 81 and filtered the group out.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE tab0 (col0 INTEGER, col1 INTEGER, col2 INTEGER);
SELECT DISTINCT -col1 AS col1 FROM tab0 GROUP BY col2, col1 HAVING NOT AVG(DISTINCT -col2) <= (+col1);

cases.name: distinct-having-base-col-wins
cases.description: Task #92 regression (minimized) — the shadow-collision rule applies to simple HAVING comparisons too. `HAVING x > 0` with alias `-x AS x` under DISTINCT must compare the BASE x (positive input values), not the aliased -x.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (10), (20);
SELECT DISTINCT -x AS x FROM t GROUP BY x HAVING x > 0 ORDER BY x;

cases.name: non-distinct-having-alias-still-wins
cases.description: Task #92 regression — without DISTINCT, HAVING continues to resolve to the output alias (matching leap-c's and mainline SQLite's non-DISTINCT behaviour). Asymmetry: DISTINCT triggers an accidental double-substitution in leap-c that collapses alias-shadow-column refs back to the base column. Rust mirrors that behaviour.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (10), (20);
SELECT -x AS x FROM t GROUP BY x HAVING x > 0;

cases.name: distinct-having-non-shadowing-alias-unaffected
cases.description: Task #92 regression — the double-substitution is a no-op when the alias name does NOT collide with a base column. Here the alias `neg` never gets re-substituted because `-x` contains no bare ColumnRef named `neg`.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3);
SELECT DISTINCT -x AS neg FROM t GROUP BY x HAVING neg < -1 ORDER BY neg;
